hook_text: Ten houses on one road. Nine sit close together. One mansion at number 84 — and it just doubled your standard deviation.
clip_script: Picture ten test marks as ten houses down one road: forty-four, forty-eight, fifty, and so on — nine of them packed close together. Then, way out of town: a mansion at number eighty-four. Question: is that house officially an outlier, or does it just look suspicious? Matric maths doesn't do suspicion. It builds fences. Take the neighbourhood — the middle half of the houses, from quartile fifty to quartile fifty-eight. Width: eight. Now walk one and a half neighbourhood-widths past each end: fifty minus twelve is thirty-eight, fifty-eight plus twelve is seventy. Those are the fences. Any house past a fence is an outlier — by rule, in writing. Eighty-four? Way past seventy. Guilty. And here's why it matters: that one mansion drags the class mean from about fifty-three up to fifty-six, and it more than DOUBLES the standard deviation — from about four komma seven to over ten. One house, rewriting the whole road's story. The median? Barely blinks. So when a mansion is on the road, report the median and the interquartile range — the tools that can't be bullied.
visual_style: A dusty street of small animated houses with one glowing mansion far right; fence posts hammer in at 38 and 70, a siren flags 84, and a seesaw shows the mean lurching while the median stands still.
pacing: Calm street tour, sharp beat when the fences hammer in, verdict delivered fast, cool one-line moral.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and catch every outlier with a rule instead of a feeling.
